 Same blood, different dugouts: Brothers reunite at Korean Series
 Samsung Lions outfielder Kim Ji-chan and his older brother Kim Jun-hyeok, a KT Wiz training assistant, reunite on opposite sides of the Korean Series.
 News Team 
 News 
 Team 
 Published 
 November 9, 2026 - 3:55 p.m. 
 Modified 
 November 16, 2026 - 2:03 p.m. 
 Make us preferred on Google 
 Samsung Lions outfielder Kim Ji-chan, right, poses for a photo with his older brother Kim Jun-hyeok after a game between Samsung and KT Wiz in Daegu on Oct. 12. 
 KT WIZ 
 SUWON, Gyeonggi — Kim Ji-chan, a newly crowned Korean Series champion with the Samsung Lions, stands at just 163 centimeters (5 feet, 4 inches), making him one of the shortest players in Korean professional baseball history. Once told he was too small to succeed at the highest level, he defied the odds through hard work and determination. He turned his small stature into an advantage and earned a regular spot on Korea's national baseball team.
 But he is not the only baseball player in the family. His older brother, Kim Jun-hyeok, who stands just 2 centimeters taller, took a slightly different path. After hanging up his uniform early, he found a new role in the sport as a training assistant for the KT Wiz.
 In the best-of-seven series that ran from Nov. 3 to Nov. 8, the brothers found themselves on opposite sides, with 25-year-old Ji-chan playing for Samsung and 27-year-old Jun-hyeok supporting KT from behind the scenes.

 The JoongAng Ilbo caught up with them at KT Wiz Park in Suwon, Gyeonggi, on Nov. 3, ahead of Game 1 of the Korean Series.
 Similar in both build and facial features, the brothers began playing baseball together in elementary school. They joined the Icheon Little League team when Jun-hyeok was in fifth grade, and Ji-chan was in third grade.
 "Actually, I didn't like baseball in the beginning," Ji-chan recalled. "My older brother started playing first, following our father, and I ended up tagging along, almost reluctantly."
 The older brother also recalled the years he and his younger brother spent playing baseball together at the same schools. 
 "We went to the same elementary, middle and high schools," Jun-hyeok said with a laugh. "Our managers and coaches were very fond of us. My younger brother, in particular, was always a well-behaved kid who never caused trouble."
 Two years apart in age, the brothers even formed a middle-infield duo at Raon High School.
 But their paths diverged after graduation. Jun-hyeok went on to Konkuk University. Ji-chan, meanwhile, was selected by Samsung in the second round of the 2020 KBO rookie draft.
 Samsung Lions leadoff hitter Kim Ji-chan celebrates after beating out an infield single in the top of the first inning against KT Wiz in Game 1 of the Korean Series at KT Wiz Park in Suwon, Gyeonggi, on Nov. 3. 
 YONHAP 
 When Ji-chan made his professional debut, he drew attention as one of the shortest players in KBO history, sharing the distinction with Samsung teammate Kim Seong-yoon, who is also 163 centimeters.
 Despite his small stature, he quickly made his mark both offensively and defensively, securing a regular spot in the lineup early in his career. Today, his name is almost always in the conversation whenever Korea selects outfielders for its national team.
 Meanwhile, Jun-hyeok finished his playing career at Konkuk University and completed his mandatory military service.
 "Even while working part-time jobs after my discharge, I didn't want to lose my connection to baseball," Jun-hyeok said. "I started looking for opportunities to work for a professional club, and this year I joined KT's minor league staff."
 Jun-hyeok initially worked as a performance analyst. But word soon spread that he was particularly good at throwing batting practice.
 His pitches were known for being sharp and challenging to hit, and in September, he was promoted to the first-team staff. That opportunity eventually brought him all the way to the Korean Series.
 Then, as fate would have it, Samsung advanced through the playoffs to face KT in the championship series, which set the stage for a reunion between the brothers.
 "I think our parents will probably root for Samsung because that's where my younger brother plays," Jun-hyeok said with a laugh. "We're not facing each other as players, but it's still amazing to meet like this. I've worried a lot because my brother has been injured so often. I just hope he can play well in this Korean Series without getting hurt."
 Samsung Lions outfielder Kim Ji-chan, right, and his older brother Kim Jun-hyeok, a training assistant for the KT Wiz, meet briefly ahead of Game 1 of the Korean Series on Nov. 3. 
 KO BONG-JUN 
 Their unusual reunion also became a talking point among KT players.
 Whenever Jun-hyeok walked by, KT players affectionately teased him, asking if he'd been to see his younger brother.
 For Ji-chan, facing a team that employs his older brother is equally meaningful. But he also feels a tinge of regret that they never had the chance to compete against each other as professional players.
 "When my brother played at Raon High School, our school didn't get much attention," Ji-chan said. "The baseball team was still very new, having been founded in 2016, so there were a lot of challenges."
 "I still don't understand why my brother, who was such a good player, never got drafted. I feel like he was born at the wrong time. If he were coming up now, I think he'd be playing professionally."
 Ji-chan also expressed pride in his older brother's dedication to his new role.
 "We may not wear the same uniform now, but I've heard that my brother is working really hard as a team staff member," he said. "That's exactly what I expected from him. He was always diligent as a player, and I hope his abilities will be recognized in his work on the field as well."
 BY KO BONG-JUN [kim.jiye@joongang.co.kr]
